title: Evaluating Factual Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
author: AI Systems Evaluation Group
content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) reduces factual hallucination rates by 41% compared with a non-retrieval baseline. The evaluation was conducted using 200 held-out questions from a medical knowledge base. The evaluation was limited to a small, single-domain dataset, so the results may not generalize to other domains.
evidence: 200 held-out questions from a medical knowledge base
limitation: Small, single-domain dataset; results may not generalize to other domains
relevance: Establishes a peer-reviewed empirical baseline for hallucination reduction in constrained domain QA

title: Scaling Enterprise Retrieval: Practical Production Insights
author: not stated in source
content: In production deployments, implementing a Retrieval-Augmented Generation layer improves generative accuracy by 35% across live enterprise workflows. Our evaluation was established via an internal A/B test over 10,000 support tickets. While effective, the underlying dataset is proprietary to enterprise customer support and baseline model configurations were not released.
evidence: Internal A/B test over 10,000 support tickets
limitation: Proprietary unreleased dataset, internal evaluation without baseline model disclosure
relevance: Demonstrates operational vendor claims and production accuracy metrics; lower-tier evidence requiring disclosure

title: Latency Overhead and Inference Cost in Augmented Language Systems
author: not stated in source
content: An independent benchmark across five open-source RAG pipelines demonstrates that adding document retrieval introduces 200–400 ms latency overhead per inference request. Tests were conducted on standard cloud GPU serving infrastructure using vector similarity search. The study focuses purely on latency and serving throughput, and did not evaluate hallucination or factual accuracy.
evidence: Benchmark across five open-source RAG pipelines
limitation: Cloud benchmark infrastructure only; factual accuracy and hallucination rates were not measured
relevance: Quantifies the computational latency trade-off inherent in deploying retrieval augmentation

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Under Complex Multi-Hop Reasoning: An Empirical Contradiction
author: not stated in source
content: Controlled evaluation indicates that Retrieval-Augmented Generation does NOT reduce factual hallucination by 41% as reported in single-domain trials. Under complex multi-hop reasoning, RAG increases factual hallucination rates by 12% to 15% compared with a baseline LLM. The trial was conducted on 8,000 multi-hop reasoning questions across four distinct domains; irrelevant retrieved passages injected distraction into the generation context. The investigation was strictly focused on multi-step reasoning tasks and excluded single-hop lookups.
key_claim: RAG does not reduce hallucination by 41%; hallucination rates increase by 12% to 15% on complex multi-hop reasoning tasks (Directly contradicts S1)
evidence: Controlled empirical trial on 8,000 multi-hop reasoning questions across 4 domains
limitation: Focused specifically on multi-hop reasoning; simple single-hop lookups were excluded
relevance: Direct Assignment 1 contradiction fixture to S1; demonstrates degradation when query complexity increases
